overview: The Western Gangas ruled Gangavadi in southern Karnataka, with centres including Kolar, Manne and Talakad. They were influential regional rulers from roughly the fourth to early eleventh century, distinct from the Eastern Gangas of Odisha. This imported record covers 500 to 800, but has no polygon for 600 to 700. Its outlines are seriously incomplete: the later one omits Talakad and both omit Kolar. These map problems are not evidence that the kingdom vanished or abandoned those centres.

periods.title: The mapped centuries of Ganga rule
periods.summary: Durvinita and Sripurusha belong to this interval; the dynasty began earlier and continued after it.

items.text: Sripurusha was a major eighth-century ruler, contending with Pallava and Rashtrakuta power. His successors increasingly ruled under Rashtrakuta supremacy. Regional kingship could survive a change of overlord: alliances, military service and family rivalries mattered alongside the boundaries drawn on a modern map.

A sixth-century copper-plate grant identifies Durvinita as the son of Avinita and the Punnata princess Jyestha. Naming both parents placed the king within two political families. Such genealogies advertised legitimacy, while giving historians evidence for connections between neighbouring ruling houses.

The same grant records a birthday gift: Durvinita awarded the village Kodungervur to two Brahmin recipients in his fortieth regnal year. A royal birthday could produce a legal document about land and income. This was a rather larger present than a parcel with a ribbon.

Five copper sheets were fastened through a ring bearing an elephant seal. The text is Sanskrit, written in a late Brahmi script. Metal preserved the transaction and the dynasty’s emblem together. Imagine carrying this version of a document folder: there was no lightweight paper inside.

Another Durvinita charter, from Hebbata and dated to his thirty-first regnal year, was reportedly found after heavy rain exposed its ring among roadside stones. Srikanta Sastri’s publication describes how the connected plates were recovered. It is a separate discovery from the fortieth-year birthday grant.

Inscriptions studied across the Ganga period distinguish dry fields, wet fields and gardens. That mattered to work and water requirements: a rain-fed plot and irrigated paddy land were different resources. Shivaramu’s study also records rice, oilseeds, sugarcane, vegetables, fruit and spices, rather than one uniform regional diet.

Keeping irrigation working meant maintaining embankments and sluices as well as digging tanks. Ganga-period records describe contributions from officials, cultivators and other local landholders. A reservoir was an ongoing shared responsibility; the difficult work continued after it was built.

Later Ganga records, after this map’s endpoint, reward tank upkeep with land or tax concessions called bittuvatta. At Karya, an endowment supported two named tanks, Piriyakere and Devigere. Maintenance received a continuing economic provision instead of depending solely on a one-time act of royal generosity.

Historian Yogender Dayma links Ganga urban growth to expanding cultivation, revenue collection and the demand generated by rulers and religious establishments. His study examines Perura, Kovalalapura, Manyapura and Talavanapura. Fields, markets and institutions supported one another; courtly life depended on goods and services arriving from elsewhere.

sections.title: An uncle’s gift and words carved in stone

items.text: An eighth-century Kannada inscription near Honnudike describes a gift by Sripurusha’s paternal uncle, Shivamara-Ereyappor. Income received during harvest offerings was assigned in gold to a local goddess. Royal kinship, farming income and local worship appear together in a short stone record.

Line two contains “kīru-tandeyar”, the editor’s Latin-letter transcription of a Kannada expression for the father’s younger brother. It comes from this particular eighth-century Honnudike inscription. The sample preserves the published reading, rather than pretending modern printed letters reproduce the ancient carving. Even an uncle could leave a linguistic trace.

The same record names collective witnesses, including a group of forty, merchants and other local participants, although parts are damaged. Making a grant involved people who could remember and recognize it. The inscription’s warning against undoing the gift shows that future disputes were very much on the donor’s mind.

sections.title: Religious places, learning and later discoveries

items.text: A seventh- or eighth-century Kulagana record describes two paddy fields, a garden, a house and a building site donated to a Jain establishment with Sivamara I’s consent. Such support joined religious activity to everyday cultivation and property. A sanctuary needed resources as well as a sacred image.

An eighth-century inscription at Nandi describes a Jain shrine and caves suitable for ascetics. The architectural discussion identifies three chambers, one behind another, and a possible seat for a teacher or image. The interpretation is tentative, but it shows how inscriptions and surviving spaces can be studied together.

The dynasty’s literary patronage continued after 800. In 978, its minister Chamundaraya composed a Kannada account of 63 exemplary figures from Jain tradition, adapting a Sanskrit work. Translation and retelling helped religious literature circulate across languages. This later achievement belongs to the kingdom’s longer history.

Excavation near Talakad’s Keertinarayana temple found earlier occupation beneath later construction. The ASI report says Hoysala building work disturbed Chola-Ganga habitation layers containing brick fragments and pottery. These mixed deposits cannot supply a neatly isolated Ganga household, but they demonstrate the city’s accumulated history.

ending.text: The Gangas continued beyond 800, often within Rashtrakuta political networks. Around 1000, Chola expansion and the rise of new regional powers ended the main Talakad kingdom. Other Ganga branches survived, while settlements, Kannada writing and Jain institutions continued under changing rulers. The map’s endpoint marks neither that conquest nor the disappearance of the population.
